newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Paris to Asia air cargo rates stable, autumn uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Paris to Asia air cargo rates stable, autumn uncertain.

text.p: With ex-Paris rates to the Far East stable over the past month or so, the prospect of autumn rises has brought a cautious response from airlines and forwarders, a Reuters survey showed.

In contrast to the Bank of France's most recent monthly bulletin on French industrial activity, which pointed to a "vigorous" flow of orders from English-speaking and Asian countries, air cargo industry sources stressed the mediocrity of current economic conditions.

"Economic growth is just not there at the moment and for air cargo this is represented by demand fluctuating from one month to the next and slack capacity. While general rates are holding up, there is a little difficulty in negotiating competitive rates with airlines for spot shipments, particularly between 500 kg and one tonne. There is no certainty that rates will increase in the autumn," said Daniel Tourigny, Paris air cargo manager of forwarders, Gondrand.
Another French forwarder, Tous Transport Aeriens (TTA), one of France's leading air forwarding agents, offered a similar viewpoint on the rates outlook.
"With a few exceptions, we see little scope for rates increases in the autumn given the depressed state of French exports," TTA managing director Alain Meister told Reuters.

He added: "This factor and the overcapacity it has caused, as well as fierce competition among carriers and the relatively high level of rates on some routes - Seoul and Hong Kong, for example - will leave little room for manoeuvre."
Commenting on Japan, Meister added stagnation in the country's air cargo imports from France would hardly be helped by sales tax increases applied from April 1.
Japan Airlines (JAL), the principal maindeck carrier on the prime Paris-Tokyo route, said it was a little premature to contemplate rates increases in the autumn.

"While cargo load factors are satisfactory it's a stable rather than a growing market. At best, we'd like to increase rates in October but if the conditions aren't right, these will probably be postponed until January 1998.
Certainly, in the last fortnight of June there were signs of the market picking up," said JAL's Paris-based cargo manager France, Francis Clement.
JAL last increased its Paris rates in January 1997.
Another leading French forwarder, SCAC Air, said it expected increases on selected Far East routes from Paris in September/October but nothing too significant.
"Rates to Singapore are likely to go up creating a better parity with Hong Kong which are relatively high," SCAC Air's managing director, Herbert de St Simon, told Reuters.

Singapore is one route from Paris where capacity has risen significantly in recent months with Air France and Singapore Airlines (SIA) upgrading their joint 747F service from three weekly frequencies to five.
"We'd like to increase rates in the autumn but that really depends on what the other major players on Far East routes are doing," said SIA's London-based cargo manager Europe, David Lim.
He added that the performance of the additional Paris freighter frequencies was satsifactory but at the same time, below expectations. However, there was no question of cutting capacity on the route.
"We are a little disappointed but we'll perserve with the situation. It's not our method to introduce extra frequencies and then do the opposite a few months afterwards."

Air France Cargo said it would not be finalising its decision on rates for the autumn period until end-July or early August. "It's a little early to speculate although at first glance there's probably scope for a significant increase to Singapore given that the last time we raised them on this route was autumn 1996.
Overall, there is now a well-set stability about ex-Paris rates," said Air France Cargo's director of Sales France, Philippe de Crecy.

Another Far East carrier, operating in the North Asia sector said: "The market is fluctuating too much for any airline to make a decision to increase rates three months in advance. They are holding on to what they have and will not jeopardise it by making noises on raising rates in the autumn out of fear of losing business. The situation is as delicate as that."
